# Cyclic Sieving for cyclic codesThanks: This research was carried out as part of the 2017 REU program at the School of Mathematics at University of Minnesota, Twin Cities. The authors are grateful for the support of NSF RTG grant DMS-1148634.

**Authors:** Alex Mason Address: Department of Mathematics, University of Washington, Seattle WA 98105, USA Email address: acmason@uw.edu , Victor Reiner Address: School of Mathematics, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN 55455, USA Email address: reiner@umn.edu and Shruthi Sridhar Address: Department of Mathematics, Princeton University, Princeton NJ 08544 Email address: ssridhar@math.princeton.edu

## Abstract

Prompted by a question of Jim Propp, this paper examines the cyclic sieving phenomenon (CSP) in certain cyclic codes. For example, it is shown that, among dual Hamming codes over ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}$ , the generating function for codedwords according to the major index statistic (resp. the inversion statistic) gives rise to a CSP when $q=2$ or $q=3$ (resp. when $q=2$ ). A byproduct is a curious characterization of the irreducible polynomials in ${\mathbb{F}}_{2}[x]$ and ${\mathbb{F}}_{3}[x]$ that are primitive.

#### 1991 Mathematics Subject Classification

## 1. Introduction

The Cyclic Sieving Phenomenon describes the following enumerative situation. One has a finite set $X$ having the action of a cyclic group $C=\langle c\rangle=\{1,c,c^{2},\ldots,c^{n-1}\}$ of order $n$ , and a polynomial $X(t)$ in ${\mathbb{Z}}[t]$ that not only satisfies $\#X=X(1)$ , but furthermore every element $c^{d}$ in $C$ satisfies

$$ \#\{x\in X:c^{d}(x)=x\}=\left[X(t)\right]_{t=\left(e^{\frac{2\pi i}{n}}\right)^{d}}. $$

In this case, one says that the triple $(X,X(t),C)$ exhibits the cyclic sieving phenomenon (CSP); see [8] for background and many examples. Frequently the polynomial $X(t)$ is a generating function

$$ X^{{\operatorname{stat}}}(t):=\sum_{x\in X}t^{{\operatorname{stat}}(x)} $$

for some combinatorial statistic $X\overset{{\operatorname{stat}}}{\longrightarrow}\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ . Some of the first examples of CSPs (e.g., Theorem 3.1 below) arose for the cyclic $n$ -fold rotation action on certain special collections $X$ of words $w=(w_{1},\ldots,w_{n})$ of length $n$ in a linearly ordered alphabet, with $X(q)=X^{{\operatorname{maj}}}(t)$ or $X^{{\operatorname{inv}}}(t)$ being generating functions for the major index and inversion number statistics, defined as follows:

$$ \displaystyle{\operatorname{inv}}(w) \displaystyle:=\#\{(i,j):1\leq i<j\leq n:w_{i}>w_{j}\}, \displaystyle{\operatorname{maj}}(w) \displaystyle:=\sum_{i:w_{i}>w_{i+1}}i. $$

This prompted Jim Propp to ask the question [7] of whether there are such CSPs in which $X$ is the set of codewords ${\mathcal{C}}$ for a cyclic error-correcting code. He initially observed the following instances of CSP triples $(X,X^{\operatorname{stat}}(t),C)$ where $X={\mathcal{C}}$ is a cyclic code inside ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{n}$ , and $C={\mathbb{Z}}/n{\mathbb{Z}}$ acts as $n$ -fold cyclic rotation of words, and either11 1 There is a subtlety here: one must choose a linear order arbitrarily on ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}$ to define the statistics ${\operatorname{maj}},{\operatorname{inv}}$ . However, it turns out that none of the results that we discuss here, including Propp’s observations, will depend upon this choice. ${\operatorname{stat}}={\operatorname{maj}}$ or ${\operatorname{stat}}={\operatorname{inv}}$ :

- • all repetition codes (trivially),

- • the full codes ${\mathcal{C}}={\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{n}$ ,

- • all parity check codes, and

- • all binary cyclic codes of length $7$ .

After a quick review of cyclic codes in Section 2, a few simple observations about CSPs for cyclic actions on words in Section 3 will explain all of the above CSPs, and a few more.

Section 4 addresses the more subtle examples of dual Hamming codes. Among other things, it shows that either $X^{\operatorname{maj}}(t)$ or $X^{\operatorname{inv}}(t)$ give rise to a CSP for all binary dual Hamming codes, while $X^{\operatorname{maj}}(t)$ also works for all ternary Hamming codes. The analysis leads to a curious characterization (Theorem 4.5(ii)) of which irreducible polynomials in ${\mathbb{F}}_{2}[x]$ or ${\mathbb{F}}_{3}[x]$ are primitive polynomials.

## 2. Preliminaries

We briefly review here the notions of linear codes, cyclic codes, and the examples that we will consider; see, e.g., Garrett [4] or Pless [6] for more background. Recall an ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}$ -linear code of length $n$ is an ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}$ -linear subspace ${\mathcal{C}}\subseteq{\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{n}$ . One calls ${\mathcal{C}}$ cyclic if it is also stable under the action of the cyclic group $C=\{e,c,c^{2},\ldots,c^{n-1}\}\cong{\mathbb{Z}}/n{\mathbb{Z}}$ whose generator $c$ cyclically shifts codewords $w$ as follows:

$$ c(w_{1},w_{2},\ldots,w_{n}):=(w_{2},w_{3},\ldots,w_{n},w_{1}). $$

It is convenient to rephrase this using the ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}$ -vector space isomorphism

$$ \begin{array}[]{rcl}{\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{n}&\longrightarrow&{\mathbb{F}}_{q}[x]/(x^{n}-1)\\
w=(w_{1},\ldots,w_{n})&\longmapsto&w_{1}+w_{2}x+w_{3}x^{2}+\cdots+w_{n}x^{n-1}.\end{array} $$

After identifying a code ${\mathcal{C}}\subset{\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{n}$ with its image under the isomorphism in (2.1), the ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}$ -linearity of ${\mathcal{C}}$ together with cyclicity means that ${\mathcal{C}}$ forms an ideal within the principal ideal ring ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}[x]/(x^{n}-1)$ . Hence ${\mathcal{C}}$ is the set $(g(x))$ of all multiples of some generating polynomial $g(x)$ . This means that

$$ {\mathcal{C}}=\{h(x)g(x)\in{\mathbb{F}}_{q}[x]/(x^{n}-1):\deg(h)+\deg(g)<n\} $$

and therefore $k:=\dim_{{\mathbb{F}}_{q}}{\mathcal{C}}=n-\deg(g(x)).$ The dual code ${\mathcal{C}}^{\perp}$ of a linear code ${\mathcal{C}}$ in ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{n}$ is defined as

$$ {\mathcal{C}}^{\perp}:=\{v\in{\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{n}:0=v\cdot w=\sum_{i=1}^{n}v_{i}w_{i}\}. $$

One has that ${\mathcal{C}}$ is cyclic with generator $g(x)$ if and only if ${\mathcal{C}}^{\perp}$ is cyclic with generator $g^{\perp}(x):=\frac{x^{n}-1}{g(x)},$ called the parity check polynomial for the primal code ${\mathcal{C}}$ . This implies $k=\dim_{{\mathbb{F}}_{q}}{\mathcal{C}}=\deg(g^{\perp}(x)).$

#### Example 2.1.

The cyclic code ${\mathcal{C}}$ having $g^{\perp}(x)=1+x+x^{2}+\cdots+x^{n-1}$ is called the parity check code of length $n$ (particularly when $q=2$ ). As a vector space, it is the space of all vectors in ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{n}$ with coordinate sum 0. Its dual code ${\mathcal{C}}^{\perp}$ consisting of the scalar multiples of $g^{\perp}(x)=1+x+x^{2}+\cdots+x^{n-1}$ is the repetition code. For example, the ternary ( $q=3$ ) repetition code ${\mathcal{C}}^{\perp}$ and parity check code ${\mathcal{C}}$ of length $n=2$ , and their respective generator polynomials $g^{\perp}(x),g(x)$ inside ${\mathbb{F}}_{3}[x]/(x^{2}-1)$ , are

$$ \begin{array}[]{rcr}{\mathcal{C}}^{\perp}=\{[0,0],[1,1],[2,2]\},&\text{ generated by }&g^{\perp}(x)=1+x,\\
{\mathcal{C}}=\{[0,0],[1,2],[2,1]\},&\text{ generated by }&g(x)=\frac{x^{2}-1}{1+x}=1+2x.\end{array} $$

#### Example 2.2.

Recall that a degree $k$ polynomial $f(x)$ in ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}[x]$ is called primitive if it is not only irreducible, but also has the property that the image $\bar{x}$ of the variable $x$ in the finite field ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}[x]/(f(x))$ has the maximal possible multiplicative order, namely $n:=q^{k}-1$ . Equivalently, $f(x)$ is primitive when it is irreducible but divides none of the polynomials $x^{d}-1$ for proper divisors $d$ of $n$ .

A cyclic code ${\mathcal{C}}$ generated by a primitive polynomial $g(x)$ in ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}[x]$ of degree $k$ is called a Hamming code of length $n=q^{k}-1$ and dimension $n-k$ . Its dual ${\mathcal{C}}^{\perp}$ generated by $\frac{x^{n}-1}{g(x)}$ is a dual Hamming code of length $n$ and dimension $k$ . See Example 4.3 below for some examples with $q=3$ (ternary codes) with $k=2$ and length $n=3^{2}-1=8$ .

Propp suggested looking for CSPs $(X,X(t),C)$ with $X$ a Hamming or dual Hamming code, using $X(t)=X^{\operatorname{maj}}(t)$ or $X^{\operatorname{inv}}(t)$ . This seems not to happen often for Hamming codes, but Section 4 exhibits many dual Hamming codes with such a CSP.

## 3. Preliminaries on CSPs for words

We first explain why the CSPs for full codes ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{n}$ and parity check codes are special cases of a general CSP for words, Theorem 3.1 below, which follows from a result in [8]; see [2, Prop. 17].

Let $A$ be a linearly ordered alphabet, and consider the set $A^{n}$ of all words $w=(w_{1},w_{2},\ldots,w_{n-1},w_{n})$ of length $n$ in the alphabet $A$ . As before, let the cyclic group $C=\{1,c,c^{2},\ldots,c^{n-1}\}$ act on $A^{n}$ via $n$ -fold rotation, so $c(w)=(w_{n},w_{1},w_{2},\ldots,w_{n-1})$ .

#### Theorem 3.1.

Let $X\subseteq A^{n}$ by any collection of words which is stable under the symmetric group ${\mathfrak{S}}_{n}$ acting on the $n$ positions, that is, if $w=(w_{1},\ldots,w_{n})$ in $X$ then $(w_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,w_{\sigma(n)})$ is also in $X$ for every $\sigma$ in ${\mathfrak{S}}_{n}$ . Then $(X,X^{\operatorname{stat}}(t),C)$ exhibits the CSP, where either ${\operatorname{stat}}={\operatorname{maj}}$ or ${\operatorname{stat}}={\operatorname{inv}}$ .

Note that Theorem 3.1 explains Propp’s observation of CSP triples involving either the full codes ${\mathcal{C}}={\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{n}$ or the parity check codes ${\mathcal{C}}=\{w\in{\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{n}:\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}=0\},$ since both are ${\mathfrak{S}}_{n}$ -stable inside ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{n}$ .

The next proposition analyzes how ${\operatorname{maj}}(w)$ changes22 2 A much more sophisticated analysis may be found in Ahlbach and Swanson [1]. when applying the cyclic shift $c$ to the word $w$ , and similarly for ${\operatorname{inv}}(w)$ if the alphabet $A$ is binary. In the latter case, we assume $A=\{0,1\}$ has linear order $0<1$ , and will refer to the Hamming weight ${\operatorname{wt}}(w)$ , as the number of ones in $w$ . We also use another statistic on words $w$ in $A^{n}$ , the number of cyclic descents

$$ {\operatorname{cdes}}(w):=\#\{i:1\leq i\leq n\text{ and }w_{i}>w_{i+1}\} $$

where we decree $w_{n+1}:=w_{1}$ to understand the inequality $w_{i}>w_{i+1}$ when $i=n$ . Lastly, define a $t$ -analogue of the number $n$ by this geometric series: $[n]_{t}:=1+t+t^{2}+\cdots+t^{n-1}=\frac{t^{n}-1}{t-1}.$ The following proposition is then straightforward to check from the definitions.

#### Proposition 3.2.

Let $A$ be any linearly ordered alphabet, and $w$ a word in $A^{n}$ .

- (i) The statistic ${\operatorname{cdes}}(w)$ is constant among all words within the $C$ -orbit of $w$ , and $\displaystyle{\operatorname{maj}}(c(w))$ $\displaystyle=\begin{cases}{\operatorname{maj}}(w)+{\operatorname{cdes}}(w)&\text{ if }w_{n}\leq w_{1},\\ {\operatorname{maj}}(w)+{\operatorname{cdes}}(w)-n&\text{ if }w_{n}>w_{1}\end{cases}$ $\displaystyle\equiv{\operatorname{maj}}(w)+{\operatorname{cdes}}(w)\,\bmod{n}.$

- (ii) In the binary case $A=\{0,1\}$ , one has $\displaystyle{\operatorname{inv}}(c(w))$ $\displaystyle=\begin{cases}{\operatorname{inv}}(w)+{\operatorname{wt}}(w)&\text{ if }w_{n}=1,\\ {\operatorname{inv}}(w)+{\operatorname{wt}}(w)-n&\text{ if }w_{n}=0\end{cases}$ $\displaystyle\equiv{\operatorname{inv}}(w)+{\operatorname{wt}}(w)\,\bmod{n}.$

The congruences modulo $n$ in Proposition 3.2 immediately imply the following.

#### Proposition 3.3.

When $w$ in $A^{n}$ has free $C$ -orbit, meaning that $\{w,c(w),c^{2}(w),\ldots,c^{n-1}(w)\}$ are all distinct, then one has the following congruence in ${\mathbb{Z}}[t]/(t^{n}-1)$ :

$$ X^{\operatorname{maj}}(t)\equiv t^{{\operatorname{maj}}(w)}\cdot[n]_{t^{{\operatorname{cdes}}(w)}}\,\bmod{t^{n}-1}. $$

In the binary case, one has

$$ X^{\operatorname{inv}}(t)\equiv t^{{\operatorname{inv}}(w)}\cdot[n]_{t^{{\operatorname{wt}}(w)}}\,\bmod{t^{n}-1}. $$

The next corollary then explains Propp’s observation about CSPs for binary cyclic codes $X={\mathcal{C}}$ of length $n=7$ using either $X^{\operatorname{maj}}(t)$ or $X^{\operatorname{inv}}(t)$ . The key point is that $7$ is prime. We will also frequently use the fact that the following three conditions are equivalent for positive integers $k,n$ :

- • $\gcd(k,n)=1$ .

- • $t^{\ell}[n]_{t^{k}}\equiv[n]_{t}\,\bmod{t^{n}-1}$ for all nonnegative integers $\ell$ .

- • $t^{\ell}[n]_{t^{k}}$ vanishes upon evaluating $t$ at any $n$ th root-of-unity that is not $1$ .

#### Corollary 3.4.

When $n$ is prime, every $C$ -stable subset $X\subset A^{n}$ gives rise to a CSP triple $(X,X^{\operatorname{maj}}(t),C)$ . If furthermore, $A=\{0,1\}$ , then one also has the CSP triple $(X,X^{\operatorname{inv}}(t),C)$ .

#### Proof.

Since $n$ is prime, $X$ must consist of a certain number $m$ of singleton $C$ -orbits that each consist of a single constant word, along with a list of free $C$ -orbits labeled $X_{1},\ldots,X_{r}$ , say with $C$ -orbit representatives labeled $w^{(1)},\ldots,w^{(r)}$ . Then for either statistic ${\operatorname{stat}}={\operatorname{maj}}$ or ${\operatorname{stat}}={\operatorname{inv}}$ , the polynomial $X^{\operatorname{stat}}(t)$ satisfies $\#X=X(1)$ by definition. For $c^{d}\neq 1$ in $C$ , one has

$$ \#\{x\in X:c^{d}(x)=x\}=m, $$

and so it remains to check that when $c^{d}\neq 1$ one has $\left[X^{\operatorname{stat}}(t)\right]_{t=\zeta_{n}^{d}}=m$ if $\zeta_{n}:=e^{\frac{2\pi i}{n}}$ . Since

$$ X^{\operatorname{stat}}(t)=m+\sum_{i=1}^{r}X^{{\operatorname{stat}}}_{i}(t), $$

it suffices to show for each $i=1,2,\ldots,r$ that $[X_{i}^{{\operatorname{stat}}}(t)]_{t=\zeta_{n}^{d}}=0$ .

Using Proposition 3.3, this follows for ${\operatorname{stat}}={\operatorname{maj}}$ since

$$ \displaystyle X_{i}^{{\operatorname{maj}}}(t) \displaystyle\equiv t^{{\operatorname{maj}}(w^{(i)})}\cdot[n]_{t^{{\operatorname{cdes}}(w^{(i)}}}\,\bmod{t^{n}-1} \displaystyle\equiv[n]_{t}\,\bmod{t^{n}-1} $$

where the last congruence above comes from $n$ being prime and $1\leq{\operatorname{cdes}}(w)\leq n-1$ for any non-constant word $w^{(i)}$ , so that $\gcd(n,{\operatorname{cdes}}(w))=1$ .

If $A=\{0,1\}$ , it similarly follows using Proposition 3.3 for ${\operatorname{stat}}={\operatorname{inv}}$ , as

$$ \begin{aligned} X_{i}^{{\operatorname{inv}}}(t)&\equiv t^{{\operatorname{inv}}(w^{(i)})}\cdot[n]_{t^{{\operatorname{wt}}(w)}}\,\bmod{t^{n}-1}\\
&\equiv[n]_{t}\,\bmod{t^{n}-1}.\end{aligned}. $$

The last congruence holds as $w^{(i)}$ non-constant gives $1\leq{\operatorname{wt}}(w^{(i)})\leq n-1$ so $\gcd(n,{\operatorname{wt}}(w^{(i)}))=1$ . ∎

#### Remark 3.5.

Note that Proposition 3.3 dashes any false hopes one might have that for binary words $w$ in $\{0,1\}^{n}$ , the distributions $\sum_{j=0}t^{{\operatorname{maj}}(c^{j}(w))}$ and $\sum_{j=0}t^{{\operatorname{inv}}(c^{j}(w))}$ are congruent modulo $t^{n}-1$ . This can fail for non-prime $n$ even when $w$ has a free $C$ -orbit. For example, $w=(1,0,1,1,0,0)$ has

$$ \sum_{j=0}t^{{\operatorname{maj}}(c^{j}(w))}\equiv t^{5}[6]_{t^{2}}\not\equiv t^{7}[6]_{t^{3}}\equiv\sum_{j=0}t^{{\operatorname{inv}}(c^{j}(w))}\,\bmod{t^{6}-1}. $$

Our discussion of dual Hamming codes will use another consequence of Proposition 3.3.

#### Corollary 3.6.

Suppose that a $C$ -stable subset $X\subseteq A^{n}$ of words has all non-constant words in $X$ lying in a single free $C$ -orbit, represented by the word $w$ .

- (i) Then $(X,X^{\operatorname{maj}}(t),C)$ gives rise to a CSP triple if and only if $\gcd(n,{\operatorname{cdes}}(w))=1$ .

- (ii) In the binary case, $(X,X^{\operatorname{inv}}(t),C)$ gives rise to a CSP triple if and only if $\gcd(n,{\operatorname{wt}}(w))=1$ .

#### Proof.

As in the proof of Corollary 3.4, for either statistic ${\operatorname{stat}}={\operatorname{maj}}$ or ${\operatorname{stat}}={\operatorname{inv}}$ , the CSP holds if and only if $\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}t^{{\operatorname{stat}}(c^{j}(w))}$ vanishes upon setting $t=\zeta_{n}^{d}$ for any $n^{th}$ root-of-unity $\zeta_{n}^{d}\neq 1$ . Since Proposition 3.3 implies the above sum is congruent modulo $t^{n}-1$ to $t^{{\operatorname{maj}}(w)}[n]_{t^{{\operatorname{cdes}}(w)}}$ when ${\operatorname{stat}}={\operatorname{maj}}$ , and to $t^{{\operatorname{inv}}(w)}[n]_{t^{{\operatorname{wt}}(w)}}$ in the binary case when ${\operatorname{stat}}={\operatorname{inv}}$ , the result follows. ∎

## 4. Dual Hamming codes

To understand when dual Hamming codes ${\mathcal{C}}$ exhibit a CSP, it will help to have many ways to characterize them among cyclic codes. As a precursor step, it helps to first characterize the cyclic codes for which the cyclic action on nonzero codewords is free.

#### Proposition 4.1.

A cyclic code ${\mathcal{C}}\subset{\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{n}$ with parity check polynomial $g^{\perp}(x)$ will have the $C$ -action on ${\mathcal{C}}\setminus\{{\mathbf{0}}\}$ free if and only if $\gcd(g^{\perp}(x),x^{d}-1)=1$ for all proper divisors $d$ of $n$ .

#### Proof.

First note that, since $c^{n}=1$ , whenever a codeword $w$ in ${\mathcal{C}}$ is fixed by some element $c^{d}\neq 1$ in $C$ , without loss of generality, one may assume $d$ is a proper divisor of $n$ ; otherwise replace $d$ by $\gcd(d,n)$ . When this happens, the polynomial $h(x)g(x)$ representing $w$ in ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}[x]/(x^{n}-1)$ has

$$ x^{d}h(x)g(x)\equiv h(x)g(x)\bmod x^{n}-1 $$

or equivalently $(x^{d}-1)h(x)g(x)$ is divisible by $x^{n}-1$ in ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}[x]$ . Canceling factors of $g(x)$ , this is equivalent to $(x^{d}-1)h(x)$ being divisible by $g^{\perp}(x)$ in ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}[x]$ . However, as discussed in Section 2, $h(x)$ can be chosen with degree strictly less than $k=\dim{\mathcal{C}}=\deg(g^{\perp}(x))$ , so the existence of such a nonzero $h(x)$ is equivalent to $g^{\perp}(x)$ sharing a common factor with $x^{d}-1$ . ∎

The next result compiles various equivalent characterizations of the primitive polynomials within ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}[x]$ , or equivalently, the dual Hamming codes. Although many of the equivalences are well-known (see, e.g., Garrett [3, Chap. 21], [4, Chap. 16], Klein [5, Chap. 2] for some), we were unable to find a source for all of them in the literature, so we have included the proofs here. Some of the equivalences involve the linear feedback shift register (LFSR) associated to a monic polynomial $f(x)=a_{0}+a_{1}x+a_{2}x^{2}+\cdots+a_{k-1}x^{k-1}+x^{k}$ , which is the ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}$ -linear map

$$ \begin{array}[]{rcl}\mathbb{F}_{q}^{k}&\overset{T_{f}}{\longrightarrow}&\mathbb{F}_{q}^{k}\\
{\bf x}=(x_{0},x_{1},...x_{k-1})&\longmapsto&T_{f}({\bf x})=(x_{1},...x_{k-1},x_{k})\end{array} $$

where $x_{k}:=-\left(a_{0}x_{k-1}+a_{1}x_{k-2}+\cdots+a_{k-1}x_{0}\right)$ . Starting with a seed vector ${\bf s}=(s_{0},s_{1},...s_{k-1})$ , since ${\bf s}$ and $T_{f}({\bf s})$ overlap in a consecutive subsequence of length $k-1$ , it is possible to create an infinite pseudorandom sequence $(s_{0},s_{1},\ldots,s_{k-1},s_{k},s_{k+1},\ldots)$ containing as its length $k$ consecutive subsequences all of the iterates $T_{f}^{r}({\bf s})=(s_{r},s_{r+1},\ldots,s_{r+k-1})$ .

#### Proposition 4.2.

Let $g^{\perp}(x)$ be any monic irreducible degree $k$ polynomial in ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}[x]$ that divides $x^{n}-1$ , where $n:=q^{k}-1$ . Let ${\mathcal{C}}\subset{\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{n}$ be the $k$ -dimensional cyclic code generated by $g(x)=\frac{x^{n}-1}{g^{\perp}(x)}$ . Then the following are equivalent:

- (i) The $C$ -action by $n$ -fold cyclic shifts on ${\mathcal{C}}\setminus\{{\bf 0}\}$ inside ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{n}$ is simply transitive.

- (ii) $\gcd(g^{\perp}(x),x^{d}-1)=1$ for all proper divisors $d$ of $n$ .

- (iii) $g^{\perp}(x)$ is primitive, that is, $\bar{x}$ has order $n$ in ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}[x]/(g^{\perp}(x))$ , so ${\mathcal{C}}$ is dual Hamming.

- (iv) The linear feedback shift register $T_{g^{\perp}}:{\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{k}\rightarrow{\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{k}$ has order $n$ .

- (v) With seed ${\bf s}:=(0,\cdots,0,1)$ in ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{k}$ , the iterates $\left\{T_{g^{\perp}}^{r}({\bf s})\right\}_{r=0,1,\ldots,n-1}$ exhaust ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{k}\setminus\{\bf 0\}$ .

- (vi) The pseudorandom sequence generated by $T_{g^{\perp}(x)}$ with seed ${\bf s}:=(0,\cdots,0,1)$ is $n$ -periodic, and each period contains each vector ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{k}\setminus\{\bf 0\}$ as a consecutive subsequence exactly once.

- (vii) The codeword $w$ in ${\mathcal{C}}\subset{\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{n}$ corresponding under (2.1) to $g(x)$ in ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}[x]/(x^{n}-1)$ , when repeated $n$ -periodically, has each vector of ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{k}\setminus\{\bf 0\}$ as a consecutive subsequence once per period.

#### Example 4.3.

When $q=3$ and $k=2$ , so $n=3^{2}-1=8$ , there are three degree two monic irreducibles $g^{\perp}(x)$ in ${\mathbb{F}}_{3}[x]$ , each shown here with $g(x)=\frac{x^{8}-1}{g^{\perp}(x)}$ and its corresponding word $w$ in ${\mathbb{F}}_{3}^{8}$ :

| $g^{\perp}(x)$ | $g(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{j}x^{j-1}$ | $w=(w_{1},\ldots,w_{8})$ |
|---|---|---|
| $x^{2}+1$ | $x^{6}+2x^{4}+x^{2}+2$ | $(2,0,1,0,2,0,1,0)$ |
| $x^{2}+x+2$ | $x^{6}+2x^{5}+2x^{4}+2x^{2}+x+1$ | $(1,1,2,0,2,2,1,0)$ |
| $x^{2}+2x+2$ | $x^{6}+x^{5}+2x^{4}+2x^{2}+2x+1$ | $(1,2,2,0,2,1,1,0)$ |

The first choice is not primitive, while the second and third are primitive. The non-primitive first choice $g^{\perp}(x)=x^{2}+1$ has LFSR $L_{g^{\perp}(x)}:(x_{0},x_{1})\mapsto(x_{1},x_{2})$ where $x_{2}=-(0\cdot x_{1}+1\cdot x_{0})=-x_{0}$ . Starting with seed $(0,1)$ , it has only $4$ different iterates

$$ (0,1)\mapsto(1,0)\mapsto(0,2)\mapsto(2,0)\mapsto(0,1)\mapsto(1,0)\mapsto(0,2)\mapsto(2,0)\,\,(\mapsto(0,1)\mapsto\cdots) $$

and this pseudorandom sequence $(0,1,0,2,0,1,0,2,0,1,0,2,0,1,\ldots),$ whose period is $4$ , not $n=8$ .

The primitive second choice $g^{\perp}(x)=x^{2}+x+2$ has LFSR $L_{g^{\perp}(x)}:(x_{0},x_{1})\mapsto(x_{1},x_{2})$ where $x_{2}=-(1\cdot x_{1}+2\cdot x_{0})=-x_{1}+x_{0}$ . Starting with seed $(0,1)$ it has $8$ different iterates (all of ${\mathbb{F}}_{3}^{2}\setminus\{\bf 0\})$

$$ (0,1)\mapsto(1,2)\mapsto(2,2)\mapsto(2,0)\mapsto(0,2)\mapsto(2,1)\mapsto(1,1)\mapsto(1,0)\,\,(\mapsto(0,1)\mapsto\cdots) $$

and pseudorandom sequence $(0,1,2,2,0,2,1,1,0,1,2,2,0,2,1,1,\ldots),$ whose period is $n=8$ .

#### Proof.

(i) $\Leftrightarrow$ (ii): Since both the cyclic group $C$ and ${\mathcal{C}}\setminus\{\bf 0\}$ have $n=q^{k}-1$ elements, the $C$ -action on ${\mathcal{C}}\setminus\{\bf 0\}$ is simply transitive if and only if it is free. Proposition 4.1 then implies the equivalence.

(ii) $\Leftrightarrow$ (iii): Since $g^{\perp}(x)$ is an irreducible factor of $x^{n}-1$ , having $\gcd(g^{\perp}(x),x^{d}-1)$ for all proper divisors $d$ of $n$ is the same as saying $g^{\perp}(x)$ does not divide $x^{d}-1$ for any proper divisor $d$ of $n$ . The latter is the same as saying $\bar{x}$ has order $n$ inside ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}[x]/(g^{\perp}(x))$ .

(iii) $\Leftrightarrow$ (iv): The matrix for $T_{g^{\perp}(x)}$ acting in the standard basis for ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{n}$ is the transpose of the matrix for multiplication by $\bar{x}$ acting in the ordered basis $(\bar{1},\bar{x},\bar{x}^{2},\ldots,\bar{x}^{k-1})$ for ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}[x]/(g^{\perp}(x))$ , that is, the usual companion matrix for $g^{\perp}(x)$ . Therefore they have the same multiplicative order.

(v) $\Rightarrow$ (iv): Since $T_{g^{\perp}(x)}$ has the same multiplicative order as multiplication by $\bar{x}$ in ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}[x]/(g^{\perp}(x))$ , and since $g^{\perp}(x)$ divides $x^{n}-1$ , the latter order divides $n$ . However, if the iterates $\left\{T_{g^{\perp}}^{r}(e_{k})\right\}_{r=0,1,\ldots,n-1}$ exhaust ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{k}-\setminus\{\bf{0}\}$ , then there are $n$ of them, so $T_{g^{\perp}}$ has order at least $n$ , and hence exactly $n$ .

(ii) $\Rightarrow$ (v): Assume (v) fails, that is, the $n$ iterates $\left\{T_{g^{\perp}}^{r}(e_{k})\right\}_{r=0,1,\ldots,n-1}$ do not exhaust the set ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{k}-\setminus\{\bf{0}\}$ of cardinality $n$ , so two of them are equal. Since $T_{g^{\perp}}$ is invertible, this means $T_{g^{\perp}}^{d}({\bf x})={\bf x}$ for some ${\bf x}\neq{\bf 0}$ and $1\leq d<n$ . Thus $T_{g^{\perp}}$ has an eigenvalue $\alpha$ in $\bar{{\mathbb{F}}}_{q}$ which is a $d^{th}$ root-of-unity for some proper divisor $d$ of $n$ , and hence its characteristic polynomial $g^{\perp}(x)$ has $\alpha$ as a root. But this would contradict (ii): primitivity of $g^{\perp}(x)$ implies that any of its roots $\alpha$ gives rise to an isomorphism ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}[x]/(g^{\perp}(x))\cong{\mathbb{F}}_{q}[\alpha]$ sending $\bar{x}\mapsto\alpha$ , so $\alpha$ should have order $n$ .

(v) $\Leftrightarrow$ (vi): By construction the $n$ -periodicity of the pseudorandom sequence comes from the fact that $T_{g^{\perp}}$ had the same order $n$ as $\bar{x}$ . The rest of (vi) is then a restatement of (v).

(vi) $\Leftrightarrow$ (vii): We claim that the word $w$ in (vii) is the reverse of the pseudorandom sequence in (vi). This is because the equation

$$ x^{n}-1=g^{\perp}(x)g(x)=\left(x^{k}+\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}a_{i}x^{i}\right)\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{j}x^{j-1}\right) $$

defining $g(x)$ via $g^{\perp}(x)$ makes the coefficient of $x^{m}$ vanish on both sides for $1\leq m\leq n-1$ , so

$$ w_{m-k+1}=-(a_{k-1}w_{m-k+2}+\cdots+a_{1}w_{m}+a_{0}w_{m+1})=T_{g^{\perp}}(w_{m+1},w_{m},\ldots,w_{m-k+2}). $$

Also, since $g(x)$ is monic of degree $n-k$ , the reverse $(w_{n},w_{n-1},\ldots,w_{2},w_{1})$ of $w$ will start with its initial $k$ terms being $(w_{n},w_{n-1},\ldots,w_{n-k+2},w_{n-k+1})=(0,0,\ldots,0,1)$ . In other words, this reverse of $w$ is the pseudorandom sequence of length $n$ generated by $T_{g^{\perp}(x)}$ with seed $(0,0,\ldots,0,1)$ . ∎

#### Proposition 4.4.

Let $X={\mathcal{C}}\subset{\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{n}$ be a $k$ -dimensional dual Hamming code, so that $n=q^{k}-1$ , with generator $g(x)$ , and $w$ in ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{n}$ its corresponding word. Then

- (i) $(X,X^{{\operatorname{maj}}}(t),C)$ exhibits the CSP if and only $\gcd(n,{\operatorname{cdes}}(w))=1$ .

- (ii) In the binary case, $(X,X^{{\operatorname{inv}}}(t),C)$ exhibits the CSP if and only $\gcd(n,{\operatorname{wt}}(w))=1$ .

#### Proof.

Combine the equivalence between Proposition 4.2 (i) and (iii) with Corollary 3.6. ∎

This leads to the main result of this section, whose part (ii) we find surprising.

#### Theorem 4.5.

Fix a positive integer $k$ and prime power $q$ , and let $n:=q^{k}-1$ .

- (i) Any nonzero codeword $w$ in a dual Hamming code in ${\mathcal{C}}\subset{\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{n}$ has ${\operatorname{cdes}}(w)=\frac{q-1}{2}\cdot q^{k-1}$ .

- (ii) If $q\in\{2,3\}$ , then a monic degree $k$ irreducible $g^{\perp}(x)$ in ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}[x]$ is primitive if and only if the word $w$ corresponding to $g(x)=\frac{x^{n-1}}{g^{\perp}(x)}$ under the bijection (2.1) has ${\operatorname{cdes}}(w)=\frac{q-1}{2}\cdot q^{k-1}$ .

- (iii) If $q\in\{2,3\}$ , then $(X,X^{\operatorname{maj}}(t),C)$ gives a CSP for $X={\mathcal{C}}$ any dual Hamming code.

- (iv) If $q=2$ , then $(X,X^{\operatorname{inv}}(t),C)$ gives a CSP for $X={\mathcal{C}}$ any dual Hamming code.

#### Proof.

For (i), note that part (i) of Proposition 4.2 shows that all nonzero words $w$ in ${\mathcal{C}}$ lie in the same $C$ -orbit, while part (iv) of the same proposition implies that the $n$ -periodic extension of $w$ contains every vector in ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{k}\setminus\{\bf 0\}$ exactly once as a consecutive subsequence each period. Consequently, every possible pair $(w_{i-1},w_{i})$ (with subscripts taken modulo $n$ ) contributing to ${\operatorname{cdes}}(w)$ has its location uniquely determined within an $n$ -period once we

- • choose the values $w_{i-1}>w_{i}$ in $\binom{q}{2}$ ways, and then

- • complete the length $k$ subsequence preceding it as $(w_{i-k+1},\ldots,w_{i-2},w_{i-1},w_{i})$ by choosing the preceding $k-2$ entries arbitrarily in $q^{k-2}$ ways; this is not ${\bf 0}$ in ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{k}$ since $w_{i-1}>w_{i}$ .

Thus ${\operatorname{cdes}}(w)=\binom{q}{2}\cdot q^{k-2}=\frac{q-1}{2}\cdot q^{k-1}$ .

For (ii), (iii), the crux is that if $q\in\{2,3\}$ , then $\frac{(q-1)}{2}q^{k-1}$ is a $q$ -power, so $\gcd\left(\frac{(q-1)}{2}q^{k-1},n\right)=1$ .

To deduce (iii), apply Proposition 4.4 to assertion (i) here.

To deduce (ii), assume $q\in\{2,3\}$ and ${\operatorname{cdes}}(w)=\frac{(q-1)}{2}q^{k-1}$ . We know that in ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}[x]/(g^{\perp}(x))$ , the element $\bar{x}$ has some multiplicative order $d$ dividing $n=q^{k}-1$ , and want to show $d=n$ . Since the LFSR $T_{g^{\perp}(x)}:{\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{k}\rightarrow{\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{k}$ also has order $d$ , the word $w$ will be $d$ -periodic, consisting of $\frac{n}{d}$ repeats of some word of length $d$ . Hence $\frac{n}{d}$ divides ${\operatorname{cdes}}(w)=\frac{(q-1)}{2}q^{k-1}$ . Since $\frac{n}{d}$ also divides $n$ , it divides $\gcd(\frac{(q-1)}{2}q^{k-1},n)=1$ . Hence $d=n$ as desired.

To deduce (iv), Proposition 4.4 applies once we compute the Hamming weight ${\operatorname{wt}}(w)$ . As the $n$ -periodic extension of $w$ has every binary sequence in ${\mathbb{F}}_{2}^{k}\setminus\{\bf 0\}$ occurring exactly once consecutively in a period, this implies ${\operatorname{wt}}(w)=2^{k-1}$ , and hence $\gcd(n,{\operatorname{wt}}(w))=\gcd(2^{k}-1,2^{k-1})=1$ , as desired. ∎

#### Example 4.6.

The assertion of Theorem 4.5(ii) fails for $q=5$ at $k=3$ . The cubic irreducible $g^{\perp}(x)=1+x+x^{3}$ in ${\mathbb{F}}[x]$ is not primitive, since $\bar{x}$ has order $d=62$ in ${\mathbb{F}}_{5}[x]/(g^{\perp}(x))$ , rather than $n=5^{3}-1=124$ . However, one can check that the word $w$ corresponding to $g(x)=\frac{x^{124}-1}{g^{\perp}(x)}$ still has ${\operatorname{cdes}}(w)=50=\frac{5-1}{2}\cdot 5^{3-1}$ . Likewise the assertion fails for $q=7$ at $k=2$ . The irreducible quadratic $g^{\perp}(x)=6+x+x^{2}$ in ${\mathbb{F}}_{7}[x]$ is not primitive, as $\bar{x}$ has order $16$ in ${\mathbb{F}}_{7}[x]/(g^{\perp}(x))$ , not $n=7^{2}-1=48$ , but one can check that the word $w$ corresponding to $g(x)$ has ${\operatorname{cdes}}(w)=21=\frac{7-1}{2}\cdot 7^{2-1}$ .

One can also check that the assertion of Theorem 4.5(iv) fails for $q=3$ at $k=2$ , such as in Example 4.3 with the choice of primitive polynomial $g^{\perp}(x)=x^{2}+x+2$ as the parity check for a dual Hamming code $X={\mathcal{C}}$ : no matter how one orders the alphabet ${\mathbb{F}}_{3}=\{0,1,2\}$ to define ${\operatorname{inv}}$ in $X^{{\operatorname{inv}}}(t)$ , the triple $(X,X^{\operatorname{inv}}(t),C)$ does not exhibit the CSP.

## 5. Questions

We close with some questions that we have not seriously explored.

#### Question 5.1.

Can one characterize the dual Hamming codes $X={\mathcal{C}}$ for which $(X,X^{\operatorname{maj}}(t),C)$ or $(X,X^{\operatorname{inv}}(t),C)$ exhibits a CSP? To what extent does this depend upon the choice of primitive polynomial parity check polynomial $g^{\perp}(x)$ and/or the linear ordering of ${\mathbb{F}}_{q}$ used to define ${\operatorname{maj}},{\operatorname{inv}}$ ?

#### Question 5.2.

Do other cyclic codes (e.g., Reed-Solomon, BCH, Golay) exhibit interesting CSPs?
